$comment: The curated toolchain manifest. PRODUCT SOURCE, not user or repository input: a repository's
.mainguard/toolchain may name an `id` from this file and nothing else. It can never supply a URL,
a package list, a command or a version — that asymmetry is what keeps a repo-writable file from
becoming an install-time code-execution surface, and making the INSTALLED SET a human's choice
Adding an entry: pin a version-addressed HTTPS tarball, paste the checksum UPSTREAM publishes
(never one computed from your own download — that is circular), and give it a probe that proves
the toolchain RUNS rather than that a file arrived. ToolchainManifestTests parses this file, so a
bad edit fails CI rather than a user's install.

toolchains.summary: CPython 3.12 with pip — runs a repository's Python test suite and installs its dependencies from PyPI.
$comment-payload: python-build-standalone (astral-sh), the same distribution `uv` installs. Chosen over the
pinned nixpkgs for one measured reason: nixpkgs' python3 — which the agent base image already
bakes at /opt/toolchain/bin/python3 — ships WITHOUT pip, and `nix profile install` cannot
express `python3.withPackages (ps: [ps.pip])` as a flake attribute path. Verified in a real
container: `import pip` fails on the base image's interpreter and `apt` cannot fix it (the
rootfs is read-only). Without a package manager a Python repository can commit tests that can
never run, which is the defect this entry closes.
These builds are also RELOCATABLE, which is what lets a toolchain be a read-only bind mount
instead of an image layer: sys.prefix is derived from the executable's own path at runtime.
Verified: extracted to an arbitrary directory and mounted read-only into the hardened jail, it
reports its own mount point as sys.prefix and pip resolves against it.
sha256 is upstream's, from the release's SHA256SUMS asset. Refresh: bump the release tag and
the version, and paste the new line from that same SHA256SUMS file.
$comment-path: The interpreter's own bin, then the per-agent user base's bin — that second entry is what puts
console scripts (`pytest`, `ruff`, `mypy`) on PATH after a project installs them, since the
toolchain itself is read-only and nothing can ever be installed into it.
$comment-environment: PYTHONUSERBASE + PIP_USER send every `pip install` into the per-agent package cache: an ext4
tree outside /workspace (so `git add -A` cannot commit a dependency closure into the branch
under verification) and outside $HOME (a 256 MiB tmpfs that a real closure overruns). This is
the same treatment NUGET_PACKAGES already gets from PackageCachePolicy, and it is what makes a
read-only toolchain usable rather than merely safe.
PIP_USER=1 is what lets a repository's verify command read `pip install -r requirements.txt`
with no Mainguard-specific flags. It is overridden by an explicit --target/--prefix and it is
refused inside a virtualenv, so a repository that builds its own venv must unset it; that is
documented in docs/design/python-toolchain.md rather than papered over.
PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE keeps __pycache__ out of the worktree — the tree under verification
must not gain untracked files that an agent's `git add -A` would then commit.
$comment-probe: Deliberately NOT `python3 --version`. Two reasons, both measured. First, the base image already
carries a python3 on PATH, so a bare version probe can pass while this toolchain is entirely
absent. Second, the defect being closed is a MISSING PIP, not a missing interpreter — a probe
that does not import pip would have reported the owner's broken environment as healthy. This
runs the toolchain's own interpreter by absolute path and imports pip in the same breath.

command: import pip, sys; print(sys.version.split()[0] + ' pip ' + pip.__version__)
